Storm Watch is a free browser game for kids 7–12 that puts them in command of a Moon base at the lunar south pole while real solar storms are coming.

When a flare hits the players have its real warning time to get their four-person crew into the shelter. They also split a limited power budget between the radiation shield and life support. Shielding slows oxygen, water and food production, and oxygen comes from splitting water, so no choice is free. Storms break machines and each repair is a short minigame. Crew who pass NASA’s 600 mSv career limit are grounded

The game is built on NASA data: flares from DONKI (the first storm is the latest real one), consumption rates from NASA’s life-support baseline (BVAD) and health facts from OSDR. In 1972 a huge solar storm hit the Moon between Apollo missions. As Artemis returns, Storm Watch helps the next generation practise the decisions astronauts will face
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Storm Watch is a free browser game where kids aged 7–12 command a Moon base at the lunar south pole through five real solar storms from NASA’s space weather database (DONKI). The first storm is always the latest big flare NASA has recorded.

Players manage four crew members: a Commander they design, plus an engineer, a botanist and a geologist. When it’s calm, they send crew outside to collect samples, which scores points but leaves them unprotected. When a flare is detected, a countdown shows the real warning time from NASA’s records, and players must get everyone into the Storm Shelter. During the storm, they split one limited power budget between the radiation shield and life support. Shielding slows oxygen, water and food production, and the base makes oxygen by splitting water, so saving air costs water. Storms break machines, and each repair is a short minigame: patching water leaks, cleaning air scrubbers, protecting the greenhouse and rebooting the solar panels. Crew who pass NASA’s 600 mSv career radiation limit are grounded. After each storm, a debrief shows what each choice cost, along with a NASA fact and a quiz question.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Kids experience real mission trade-offs instead of memorizing facts, because every option has a cost. Science words like “dose” and “regolith” can be tapped for a short explanation. Three difficulty levels (Cadet, Pilot and Commander) let a 7-year-old and an older sibling both find a challenge. A different storm each round, changing quiz questions and 19 collectible fact cards make it replayable. It runs on any computer or phone with no download or account, so a classroom can use it in a single lesson. As Artemis returns people to the Moon, Storm Watch gives the next generation early practice in the decisions astronauts will face.

TOOLS

JavaScript, HTML5 Canvas and CSS, with no game engine. The Web Audio API generates every sound, and the Web Speech API voices Mission Control. NASA data: DONKI, the Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document (BVAD), the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), NASA-STD-3001, LRO, LCROSS, MAVEN and Curiosity RAD. We also used Chang’e-4 radiation data and DiceBear avatars. Built with Node.js, tested with Playwright, hosted on Firebase, managed on GitHub. Claude (AI) assisted with coding and writing.

CREATIVITY

Real storms with their real warning times turn a historical dataset into a countdown players can feel. Every repair is its own small game. The team appear as the crew in the game. The ending shows the 2017 storm lighting up Mars while the surviving crew wave from the Moon. The scene matches the south pole: a low Sun, upright solar panels and water ice underground.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Young players’ attention: short sessions, plain words, big touch targets, and fact cards that pause the game. Not too many systems: one power budget and one radiation bar. No free choices. Scientific honesty: every source is credited in the game, saved data is labeled as saved, and we say openly that storm strength is tuned so kids can win. No NASA logos, and cartoon avatars instead of real photos.
